q: Wine blended from Cachapoal and Colchagua may be sold under which single umbrella denomination?
exp: Rapel is the parent name for both. Cachapoal lies to the north and Colchagua to the south, separated by a low range of hills.

q: Warm, clay-rich ground in Cachapoal has become the reference address for Chile's signature red. Which sector is it?
exp: Peumo gives Carmenere the heat and the long season the variety demands. Picked too soon it turns hard and green, so the site has to buy the grower time.

q: A horseshoe of granitic hillside in Colchagua, curled around a river bend and planted to Syrah, Carmenere and Cabernet, is known as what?
exp: Apalta's slopes give poorer, better-drained soil than the valley floor and a natural amphitheatre of exposures. It is the single most quoted name in Colchagua.

q: A Catalan producer arrived in 1979 with stainless steel and temperature control, and the date is often taken as the start of the modern Chilean industry. Where did he settle?
exp: Miguel Torres set up in Curico and Chilean whites in particular were transformed inside a decade. Curico's Lontue and Teno sub-valleys remain a large source of everyday wine.

q: Dry-farmed bush vines planted after the earthquake of 1939 underpin a growers' association in Maule. Which variety do they champion?
exp: Carignan was brought in to add colour and acid to Pais after the quake wrecked the region's cellars. VIGNO now bottles it from old unirrigated vines and has made Maule a serious name again.

q: Running from north to south, which order correctly places the four sub-regions of Chile's Central Valley?
exp: Santiago sits at the northern end beside Maipo, and Maule marks the southern boundary of the Central Valley proper. Everything below it belongs to the Southern Regions.

q: Morning fog, cold nights and a real risk of spring frost make one valley between Santiago and the sea Chile's white wine pioneer. Which?
exp: Planted from the early 1980s on ground nobody had thought suitable for vines, Casablanca proved Chile could make cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay. Frost is the price of the cold air that pools there.

q: Planting the Leyda Valley became viable only once water was piped several kilometres from a neighbouring river. Which obstacle did that remove?
opts: The slopes were too steep to work without terracing
The soils were too saline until they had been flushed
There was too little rainfall for vines
Frost could not be fought without sprinkler water
exp: San Antonio and its Leyda sub-valley lie a few kilometres from the Pacific, which supplies the cold and the wind but not the water: without irrigation there is far too little rainfall to establish a vineyard there. The pipeline opened one of Chile's best sites for Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir.

q: Calcareous soils, near-desert rainfall and ocean fog have made one far northern valley Chile's source of taut Chardonnay and cool-climate Syrah. Which?
exp: Limestone is scarce in Chilean vineyards and Limari has it. The valley opens straight to the sea, so the camanchaca reaches a long way inland.

q: Chile's northernmost vineyards share their valleys with the stills that make the national spirit. Which spirit is that?
exp: Elqui is pisco country, distilled largely from Muscat varieties, and its wine vineyards climb high above the valley floor. Cachaca is Brazilian and Singani Bolivian.

q: A warm east-west valley named for the highest peak in the Americas built its reputation on Cabernet and Syrah grown at Panquehue. Which valley?
exp: The Aconcagua valley runs inland from the coast north of Santiago and is one of Chile's warmest quality zones. Its cool coastal sector, Aconcagua Costa, is a far more recent development.

q: Ungrafted bush vines of Pais, some of them centuries old, alongside old dry-farmed Cinsault, are concentrated in which southern zone?
exp: Itata holds Chile's oldest vineyards, farmed on the dry hills of the secano interior. Bio-Bio and Malleco further south are cool and wet enough for Riesling, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

q: Much of what Chile exported as Merlot before 1994 turned out to be a different Bordeaux variety. Which one?
exp: Carmenere had been interplanted with Merlot for a century and nobody had pulled the two apart. Chile now grows more of it than anywhere else and treats it as a national signature.

q: Which discipline, working from the shape of leaves and shoots in the vineyard, first showed that Chile's Merlot was not all Merlot?
exp: The French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot made the call in 1994 and DNA work confirmed it. Pedology is the study of soils and phenology the timing of the vine's growth stages.

q: Picked on the same day as the Merlot beside it, Carmenere shows a hard green capsicum note. What is the cause?
opts: Residual sugar left in the wine
exp: Those pyrazines fall away only after several more weeks of ripening. Carmenere ripens very late, often into May in Chile, and the whole art of it is holding your nerve. Underripe fruit gives the green streak the variety was once notorious for.

q: Spanish missionaries carried a black variety through the Americas in the sixteenth century, and in Chile it still fills jugs of country wine. What is it called there?
exp: The same vine is Mission in California, Criolla Chica in Argentina and Listan Prieto in Spain. Old dry-farmed Pais is now bottled seriously, often by carbonic maceration.
